title: From Grandpa's Workshop to Satellite Circuits: Ana Inês Inácio's Blueprint for the Future of Wireless
summary: Most of us never think about the radio waves crisscrossing the air around us. But for Ana Inês Inácio, those invisible signals are a canvas. At the Netherlands Organization for Applied Scientific Research (TNO) in The Hague, she designs integrated circuits—the tiny, hyper-specialized chips that will form the backbone of tomorrow's radar and satellite communication systems. Her work recently earned her the IEEE-Eta Kappa Nu Outstanding Young Professional Award, a prestigious honor recognizing not just her technical prowess but her leadership in building global engineering communities. Inácio's path to RF engineering began far from high-tech labs, in the rural Portuguese village of Vales do Rio. Her grandfather repaired industrial looms in the region's textile mills, teaching himself electrical systems through correspondence courses. "He would show me why something broke and how we could fix it," she recalls. That hands-on curiosity stuck. In high school, she was torn between physics and biology, but encouragement from teachers and an engineer uncle steered her toward electronics. She enrolled in a five-year integrated master's program at the University of Aveiro, and a 2012 exchange at Eindhoven University of Technology brought her to the Netherlands, where she stayed. Today, her circuits are pushing the boundaries of radio-frequency (RF) sensor systems. These systems are crucial for advanced radar—think of them as the eyes and ears of autonomous vehicles or climate-monitoring satellites. The award citation highlights her "pioneering advancements in RF sensor systems, bridging technical excellence with impactful community engagement." That community piece is no small add-on. Inácio has been a driving force in IEEE Young Professionals, creating spaces where early-career engineers can connect, collaborate, and innovate. "Sometimes that means circuits; sometimes it means helping people connect and grow together," she says. Her dual focus—on atoms and on people—offers a blueprint for how the next generation of technology leaders can build both better devices and a more inclusive field.
why_it_matters: This story shows that the technology behind your smartphone and future self-driving cars is created by people who also invest in helping others succeed – challenging the idea that engineering is just about machines, not about human connections and inclusivity.

background_read: Ana Inês Inácio works at the Netherlands Organization for Applied Scientific Research (TNO), an independent Dutch institute that develops technologies for industry and government, bridging science and real-world products.

The award she received, IEEE-Eta Kappa Nu Outstanding Young Professional, is given by a prestigious society within IEEE – the world’s largest technical professional organization – to engineers under 35 who show both technical skill and community leadership.

Radio-frequency engineering is the backbone of modern life: every Wi-Fi router, smartphone, and weather satellite depends on circuits that send and receive these invisible signals. This field took off in the mid-20th century as radar and broadcasting expanded, and it continues to evolve with 5G and space exploration.

Inácio’s path reflects a broader push for diversity in STEM fields, where women remain underrepresented. Her dual dedication to hardware and mentorship echoes trends seen in other pioneering engineers who believe technology advances fastest when everyone can contribute.

perspectives.description: Inácio’s recognition shows that young professionals can shape their fields through both innovation and mentorship. Her story can inspire students, especially girls, to see engineering as creative and people-centered.

Expecting engineers to be both technical wizards and community leaders could set an unrealistic standard, especially for underrepresented groups who already face extra hurdles. It risks making exceptional service seem like a requirement, not a choice.

The article reflects a broader shift in many technical careers, where soft skills like networking and mentoring are increasingly valued alongside hard skills. This trend may be a natural response to more collaborative, interdisciplinary projects.

If engineering communities follow Inácio’s model, they could become more diverse and supportive, leading to fewer dropouts among early-career professionals and possibly faster innovation as more voices are heard.
